title: How to Collect User Feedback on AI Agent Runs
summary: Collect user feedback on AI agent runs: tie thumbs up/down to the exact trace, add implicit signals, compare releases in SQL, and route runs to review.
body_markdown:
User feedback on an AI agent includes explicit ratings and comments, plus behavioral signals such as edits and regenerate clicks. To investigate an answer, you need to connect those signals to the run that produced it.


Consider an analytics copilot that turns "revenue by region last quarter" into SQL and summarizes the results. Three hours after a chart renders, the user clicks thumbs-down and writes "wrong region filter." The trace has ended; the feedback endpoint receives only a message ID.


If that message maps to a trace, you can inspect the generated SQL, check the data returned, and identify the release that produced the answer. This guide uses Laminar to capture that link and turn feedback into review work and release comparisons. Those comparisons help you choose what to investigate; they do not establish that a prompt change caused an improvement.


## Store the trace ID with every agent message#


Feedback often arrives in a separate request after the agent run has finished. Save the trace ID beside the message in your application database while the run is active.


In Laminar, Laminar.get_trace_id()


returns the current trace ID inside a span context, such as an @observe


d function. The entry point below sets the session and user IDs, then returns the trace ID with the answer:


```text
from   lmnr   import   Laminar  ,   observe


Laminar  .  initialize  (  )


@observe  (  name  =  "answer_question"  )
def     answer_question  (  conversation_id  :     str  ,   user_id  :     str  ,   question  :     str  )     -  >     dict  :
Laminar  .  set_trace_session_id  (  conversation_id  )
Laminar  .  set_trace_user_id  (  user_id  )
sql   =   write_sql  (  question  )
rows   =   run_query  (  sql  )
answer   =   summarize  (  question  ,   rows  )
return     {  "answer"  :   answer  ,     "sql"  :   sql  ,     "trace_id"  :     str  (  Laminar  .  get_trace_id  (  )  )  }


def     handle_question  (  conversation_id  :     str  ,   user_id  :     str  ,   question  :     str  ,   plan  :     str  )     -  >     dict  :
result   =   answer_question  (  conversation_id  ,   user_id  ,   question  )
message_id   =   db  .  insert_message  (
conversation_id  =  conversation_id  ,
trace_id  =  result  [  "trace_id"  ]  ,
sql  =  result  [  "sql"  ]  ,
answer  =  result  [  "answer"  ]  ,
plan  =  plan  ,
)
return     {  "message_id"  :   message_id  ,     "answer"  :   result  [  "answer"  ]  ,     "sql"  :   result  [  "sql"  ]  }


```


Here, write_sql


, run_query


and summarize


are application functions, each decorated with @observe


to appear as spans. db


represents your database.


The browser receives a message_id


, not the trace ID or a Laminar API key. Its feedback request posts that message ID to your backend, which looks up the trace. Call get_trace_id()


before leaving the observed function: outside a span context, it returns None


.


Keep context you will need for analysis, such as the plan or UI surface, in the message row too. Include any added fields in every metadata sync described below. The[metadata docs](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/metadata) describe this delayed-feedback pattern.


## Choose the feedback unit: turn, conversation or step#


Choose the unit before you build the button or calculate rates.


**Turn: one trace.** A vote on a message rates that turn. With one trace per user turn, the message's trace is the unit used by the handler and SQL below. A regenerate click belongs to the trace being replaced.


**Conversation: one session.** An end-of-chat rating concerns the whole conversation. Laminar groups traces into[sessions](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/sessions) by session_id


. You can anchor session feedback to the last turn's trace, using separate conversation fields and feedback_scope: "conversation"


. Keep conversation ratings separate from feedback_rating


so they do not overwrite a turn's vote. Roll up by session_id


for conversation-level reporting.


**Step: a span hint.** Editing generated SQL points you toward write_sql


, but does not prove that step failed. Post-run tags and metadata in this Laminar workflow attach to the trace. Record feedback_step: "write_sql"


as a hint, and keep track of whether the app, user or reviewer supplied it. A reviewer must still inspect the span's input and output.


Feedback Unit Where it goes


Thumbs up/down on a message Turn That message's trace


Comment on a message Turn That message's trace


End-of-conversation rating Conversation Last turn's trace, feedback_scope: "conversation"


User edits the generated SQL Step hint The message's trace, feedback_step: "write_sql"


Regenerate click Turn The trace being replaced


## Write user feedback to the finished trace in Laminar#


Laminar has no dedicated feedback score object for production traces. Use[tags](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/tags) such as feedback-negative


and needs-review


for routing. Use metadata for the rating, comment and step hint. Tags are queryable as trace_tags


; metadata is JSON.


This backend handler records a vote, comment or SQL edit in your database before syncing it:


```text
from   lmnr   import   LaminarClient


client   =   LaminarClient  (  )


def     record_feedback  (  message_id  :     str  ,     **  changes  )     -  >     None  :
db  .  update_feedback  (  message_id  ,     **  changes  )
sync_feedback  (  message_id  )


def     sync_feedback  (  message_id  :     str  )     -  >     None  :
msg   =   db  .  get_message  (  message_id  )
if   msg  .  rating   ==     -  1  :
client  .  tags  .  tag  (  msg  .  trace_id  ,     [  "feedback-negative"  ,     "needs-review"  ]  )
client  .  traces  .  push_metadata  (
msg  .  trace_id  ,
{
"plan"  :   msg  .  plan  ,
"feedback_rating"  :   msg  .  rating  ,
"feedback_comment"  :   msg  .  comment   or     ""  ,
"feedback_step"  :   msg  .  step   or     ""  ,
"sql_edited_by_user"  :   msg  .  sql_edited  ,
}  ,
)


```


rating


is 1


, -1


, or None


for a message nobody rated. Called as record_feedback(message_id, rating=-1, comment="wrong region filter", step="write_sql")


, the trace gets two tags and the full record. An edit alone, record_feedback(message_id, sql_edited=True, step="write_sql")


, writes feedback_rating: null


, which the queries below don't count as a rating.


In our tests against the current open-source Laminar server, push_metadata


replaced the entire metadata object: a push containing only sql_edited_by_user


erased an earlier rating, and a feedback push erased the plan


key set during the run. The client reference describes a shallow merge. Sending the complete record works under either behavior, as long as it includes every key you want to keep.


Treat the database as authoritative and coordinate any other metadata writers. Extend both the database record and the sync snapshot when you add fields.


Re-reading the row avoids replaying an old payload, but overlapping syncs can still land out of order. Serialize writes per message where practical, and periodically re-sync changed messages so the trace can converge after updates settle.


**Retry even without an exception.** A metadata push before trace ingestion logs a warning and returns without raising. In our test, a click recorded before the trace was flushed was skipped, and a later sync wrote it. Retry from the database, not a saved payload.


**Tags are additive.** A user who flips from thumbs-down to thumbs-up still leaves feedback-negative


and needs-review


on the trace. Treat these as historical flags and read the current rating from metadata.


Langfuse provides named, typed scores with optional comments and a browser scoring client. Braintrust's logFeedback


attaches scores, comments and metadata to a span; its feedback guide describes child spans per submission, with scores averaged on the parent. Those are more structured feedback models. In Laminar, you own the metadata schema.


## Pair explicit feedback with behavioral signals#


Explicit ratings tell you which vote a user chose, not why an answer failed. Langfuse's feedback guide describes explicit feedback as rare and skewed toward unhappy users. Unrated runs are not positive ratings.


Behavioral signals widen the pool of runs to examine, but need interpretation. A copy action could mean the answer was useful or that it is going into a bug report.


Signal Kind How to capture What it may mean


Thumbs down + comment Explicit Feedback endpoint Answer wrong or unhelpful


SQL edited before running Implicit Query editor event Look at write_sql


first


Regenerate click Implicit Backend event Answer rejected


Chart added to a dashboard Implicit Backend event Answer used


Question rephrased next turn Implicit Trace analysis Agent misunderstood


Conversation abandoned Implicit Session-level SQL Solved, or gave up


Capture backend events through the same application record, extending the sync snapshot to include their fields.


Textual signals need analysis of the run. In Laminar, a[Signal](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/introduction) combines an instruction and output schema that the Signals agent applies to finished traces matching its trigger and filters. It records a structured event when it finds a match.


The built-in **Friction** template looks for "confusion, repeated attempts, or poor user experience" and records a description and severity: low, medium or high. New projects can enable it during onboarding. It runs on traces over 1,000 tokens by default. The[Signals quickstart](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/quickstart) explains setup.


A Signal reads one trace at a time. To detect a rephrased question, that trace must contain the earlier exchange. Most chat agents resend the conversation history on every model call, so it usually does. If your application truncates or summarizes conversation history, the Signal has less evidence.


Use these signals to select runs for review, not to assign a quality score.


## When product analytics is enough#


For satisfaction trends, keep thumbs events in your existing product analytics tool, such as PostHog or Amplitude. Your PM can work in the same event and cohort workflow.


A bare click event cannot explain why the answer disappointed someone. It needs run context to reveal the SQL, returned rows or prompt version. A trace gives an engineer that context.


You can use both: send the analytics event with the trace ID as a property, and write the feedback to the trace. Product analytics tracks behavior; the linked trace supports investigation.


## Compare feedback by release and agent version#


After a prompt or tool change, compare feedback on the traces produced by each release. Treat the result as descriptive: a shift tells you where to investigate, not that the change caused it.


Laminar records a release, usually a git commit SHA, when one is supplied or detected through configuration such as LMNR_RELEASE


. It is a separate column, unaffected by metadata writes. Run this query in the[SQL editor](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/sql-editor) :


```text
SELECT
release  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
countIf  (  JSONExtractInt  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_rating'  )     IN     (  -  1  ,     1  )  )     AS   rated  ,
countIf  (  JSONExtractInt  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_rating'  )     =     -  1  )     AS   thumbs_down  ,
countIf  (  JSONExtractBool  (  metadata  ,     'sql_edited_by_user'  )  )     AS   edited  ,
round  (  rated   /   runs  ,     3  )     AS   feedback_rate  ,
round  (  thumbs_down   /   greatest  (  rated  ,     1  )  ,     3  )     AS   negative_share  ,
round  (  edited   /   runs  ,     3  )     AS   edit_rate
FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     16     DAY
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     2     DAY
AND   top_span_name   =     'answer_question'
GROUP     BY     release
ORDER     BY     min  (  start_time  )


```


The upper bound excludes the last two days to allow feedback to arrive. Choose that delay from your own feedback timing. On a test project with synthetic traffic (bound removed, since the runs were minutes old), it returned the results below. They demonstrate the query, not release quality:


release runs rated thumbs_down edited feedback_rate negative_share edit_rate


a1b2c3d 20 7 4 2 0.35 0.571 0.1


e4f5a6b 21 11 3 2 0.524 0.273 0.095


Read coverage and negative share together. feedback_rate


divides rated runs by all runs; negative_share


divides negative ratings by rated runs. With no rated runs, the query returns zero for negative_share


to avoid division by zero, not to report perfect satisfaction.


Compare releases with the same feedback UI and comparable traffic. A larger button can change who rates. These small synthetic samples cannot establish an improvement.


Laminar's[agent versions](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/agent-versions) feature is in beta. It groups LLM calls by the opening of their system prompt and records a new version when the prompt or tool definitions change. Keep the release alongside the version to identify its deployment. ARRAY JOIN


associates feedback with versions present in a trace:


```text
SELECT
v  .  version_hash   AS   version  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
countIf  (  JSONExtractInt  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_rating'  )     =     -  1  )     AS   thumbs_down
FROM   traces
ARRAY   JOIN   agent_versions   AS   v
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     16     DAY
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     2     DAY
AND   top_span_name   =     'answer_question'
GROUP     BY   version
ORDER     BY   runs   DESC


```


A trace lists all agent versions that ran in it, so a multi-agent trace's rating contributes to each version. Filtering to the agent you changed narrows the cohort; it does not turn a whole-run vote into a step-level verdict.


Implicit signals can also be compared per run. This subquery counts traces with Friction events:


```text
SELECT
release  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
countIf  (  id   IN     (
SELECT   trace_id   FROM   signal_events
WHERE   signal_name   =     'Friction'     AND     timestamp     >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     16     DAY
)  )     AS   friction  ,
round  (  thumbs_down   /   runs  ,     3  )     AS   thumbs_down_rate  ,
round  (  friction   /   runs  ,     3  )     AS   friction_rate
FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     16     DAY
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     2     DAY
AND   top_span_name   =     'answer_question'
GROUP     BY     release


```


Here, friction_rate


means flagged runs divided by all selected runs. Friction evaluates only traces passing its triggers and filters, including the default token threshold. A release with shorter traces may have lower coverage. Compare eligibility and configuration before interpreting differences, then read representative traces. These counts do not measure Friction's detection accuracy.


## Route negative runs into review and a regression dataset#


Queue candidates, not presumed defects. This query selects negative ratings, SQL edits and Friction events:


```text
SELECT
id   AS   trace_id  ,
session_id  ,
release  ,
JSONExtractInt  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_rating'  )     AS   rating  ,
JSONExtractString  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_comment'  )     AS     comment  ,
JSONExtractString  (  metadata  ,     'feedback_step'  )     AS   step  ,
JSONExtractBool  (  metadata  ,     'sql_edited_by_user'  )     AS   edited  ,
id   IN     (
SELECT   trace_id   FROM   signal_events
WHERE   signal_name   =     'Friction'     AND     timestamp     >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     7     DAY
)     AS   friction  ,
agent_input  ,
end_time
FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     7     DAY
AND   top_span_name   =     'answer_question'
AND     (  rating   =     -  1     OR   edited   OR   friction  )
ORDER     BY   end_time   DESC
LIMIT     200


```


agent_input


is the user's request as Laminar extracts it from the trace. For "wrong region filter," start with the write_sql


hint. Compare the requested region with that span's input and generated filter, then inspect the rows returned by run_query


. Decide whether the problem came from interpretation, data or a changed user requirement before proposing a fix.


From the SQL results, **Export → Export to Labeling Queue** sends rows to a[labeling queue](https://laminar.sh/docs/queues/quickstart) . A reviewer records what the agent should have done. For scheduled exports, use POST /v1/labeling_queues/{queue_id}/items


with the trace ID as idempotencyKey


; retries then return the same item instead of creating duplicates.


Approved cases can become regression tests.[How to Turn Production Traces into an Eval Dataset](https://laminar.sh/article/production-traces-to-eval-dataset) covers that workflow.


Run the regression eval to check whether the known cases pass after the fix. Then compare production feedback on mature, comparable release cohorts. Passing known cases and seeing fewer complaints provide different evidence; neither proves the change helped every workload.


## FAQ#


### Can the browser send feedback straight to Laminar?#


Route it through your backend. Tag and metadata writes require a project API key, which must stay server-side. Authenticate the request, confirm the user can access the message, and validate allowed feedback fields before calling the handler. Do not pass arbitrary request fields into **changes


.


### How late can feedback arrive and still attach to the run?#


For a finished trace still stored in the project, feedback can arrive seconds, minutes or days later if you retained its ID. A metadata push before ingestion is skipped, so delayed synchronization matters even for immediate clicks. The[client reference](https://laminar.sh/docs/sdk/client) documents the finished-trace calls.


### Can I put a human reviewer's verdict on the same trace?#


Yes. Use separate keys such as review_verdict


and review_note


, and include them in the authoritative full-record write. Keep the user's rating intact: "agent was right, data was stale" explains the complaint without erasing it. Ensure your sync worker includes reviewer fields rather than overwriting them.


### Should I use thumbs-down to tune a Signal?#


Use disagreements to select traces for review, not as labels. A thumbs-down run may be outside Friction's purpose or ineligible under its filters. A positive rating does not disprove friction. Check the trace against the instruction before discarding an event. Discarding deletes the event and adds your reason to the instruction on future runs. The[Signals quickstart](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/quickstart) explains this behavior.
